lessons.title: Selling at Local Markets and Trade Fairs
lessons.body:
Start by choosing the right market. In most African towns, the main market runs on specific daysâfor example, Tuesday and Friday in Kumasi, or Saturday in Kano. Visit as a customer first. Count how many people sell oils or cosmetics. Note what they charge. A 500ml bottle of pure coconut oil often sells for 3,000 to 5,000 Naira in Nigeria, or 30 to 50 Ghana Cedis in Ghana. Shea butter in 250g tubs goes for similar amounts. Your price should be within 10% of the average, but you can charge more if your packaging is cleaner.

Book a stall early. A good spot near the entrance or near a busy food seller costs moreâmaybe 2,000 Naira per dayâbut you will sell three times more than at the back. Bring a small table, a clean cloth, and at least 30 bottles of oil and 20 tubs of shea butter. Label everything with your phone number and a simple name like 'Amina's Pure Oils'. People trust a name.

At trade fairs, like the Lagos International Trade Fair or the Nairobi Agricultural Show, you must register weeks in advance. Fees range from 20,000 to 100,000 Naira for a small booth. But fairs attract buyers who want bulk. Offer a 'fair special': buy 10 bottles, get 1 free. Collect phone numbers of everyone who stops. Even if they don't buy, add them to your WhatsApp list.

During the market day, stand up, smile, and offer free samples. A tiny dab of shea butter on a customer's hand sells more than any words. Keep a notebook to record what sells bestâscented or unscented, small or large sizes. After the market, count your money and note what you sold. Next time, bring more of the best sellers. Always have change in small notes. And never leave your stall unattended; theft is common. With practice, you can make 20,000 to 50,000 Naira profit in a single market day.

lessons.title: Using WhatsApp and Social Media to Sell
lessons.body:
WhatsApp is the most powerful free tool for selling oils in Africa. Start by saving all your contactsâfriends, family, church members, market customersâand create a broadcast list called 'Oil Customers'. Send one message per week, not more, or people will block you. A good message has a clear photo, a short price, and a call to action. For example: 'Pure coconut oil, 500ml â 3,500 Naira. Free delivery in Surulere tomorrow. Reply YES to order.' Use natural light for photos. Put the bottle on a clean white cloth or a wooden table. Show the oil being poured or shea butter being scooped.

Create a WhatsApp Business account (free) to set up a catalogue, auto-replies, and labels like 'New Order' or 'Paid'. This makes you look professional. Also, join local WhatsApp groups for your areaâ'Buy and Sell Lagos', 'Nairobi Mums', etc. Read the group rules first. Most allow one advert per day. Post a photo with a short caption and your number. Do not spam.

For Facebook, create a page called 'YourName Coconut & Shea Oils'. Post 3 times a week: a product photo, a customer testimonial, and a short video of you making the oil. Boost a post for as little as 1,000 Naira to reach 5,000 people in your city. On Instagram, use hashtags like #SheaButterNigeria #CoconutOilGhana #NaturalHairAfrica. TikTok is great for short videosâshow how you package or use the oil. One viral video can bring 50 orders.

Always reply to messages within 1 hour. If someone asks 'How much?', answer with price, size, and delivery cost. Ask for their location and offer mobile money payment (M-Pesa, MoMo, or bank transfer). Send a payment confirmation and a thank-you message. After delivery, ask for a photo review. Post that review on your status. This builds trust. Never argue online. If a customer complains, move the chat to a private call. With consistent posting, you can sell 100 bottles a month from your phone alone.

lessons.title: Building a Customer Base in Your Community
lessons.body:
Your first customers are the people you see every day: neighbours, church members, market women, and salon owners. Start by making a list of 50 people you know. Visit them in person with a small sampleâa 50ml bottle of coconut oil or a 100g wrap of shea butter. Say, 'I made this. Try it for free. If you like it, I sell bigger sizes.' This costs you little but builds goodwill. Ask them to tell one friend. Word spreads fast in a close community.

Offer a loyalty card. A simple cardboard card works: buy 5 bottles, get the 6th free. Or give a 10% discount on every 10th purchase. Keep a notebook or use a free app like 'Loyalty Cards' on your phone. When a customer buys, write their name and number. Send them a WhatsApp message on their birthday with a small discount. People love to be remembered.

Host a 'sampling day' at your home or a community hall. Invite 20 people. Show how you make the oil. Let them smell and test. Sell at a special price for that day only. Serve water or tea. This turns customers into fans. Also, partner with local tailors, hair braiders, and barbers. Leave 5 bottles with them on consignmentâthey sell and keep 20% commission. You lose nothing if it doesn't sell.

Keep a simple record of every sale: date, name, product, amount. After one month, you will see who buys often. Send those top customers a thank-you message and a small gift (like a free lip balm). Ask them for referrals. A satisfied customer will bring 2-3 new ones. In a community, your reputation is your best advert. Always deliver on time, use clean packaging, and never sell rancid oil. If you do this, within 6 months you can have a base of 200 repeat customers who buy every month.

lessons.title: Partnering with Salons and Cosmetic Shops
lessons.body:
Salons and cosmetic shops are goldmines because they already have customers who buy oils and shea butter. Walk into 10 salons in your area. Ask to speak to the owner. Bring a sample of your best coconut oil and shea butter. Say, 'I can supply you at wholesale price. You make profit, and I give you free marketing.' Offer a wholesale price that is 30% below your retail price. For example, if you sell a 500ml bottle for 3,500 Naira, sell to the salon for 2,500 Naira. They can sell at 3,500 and keep 1,000 Naira profit.

Start with a small trial: give them 10 bottles on consignment. You get paid only when they sell. Check back in one week. If they sold, ask for a bigger order and maybe a small deposit. If not, take back the unsold bottles and try another salon. Always provide a simple invoice book. Write the date, items, quantity, and total. Both of you sign. This avoids disputes.

For cosmetic shops, offer a display stand with your brand name. You can make a simple wooden or cardboard stand. Put your phone number on it. Offer a special 'salon exclusive' scentâlike coconut oil with lavenderâthat only they sell. This makes them feel special. Also, train the salon workers on how to use your oil for hair and skin. Give them a free 1-litre bottle for their own use. Happy workers recommend your product to every client.

Organise a monthly 'salon day' where you visit, give free samples to customers, and take orders. Pay the salon owner a small commission (5%) for every customer who orders through them. This motivates them. Keep a WhatsApp group with all your salon partners. Post new stock, price changes, and tips. Within 3 months, you can have 5 regular salon partners. Each salon can sell 20 bottles a month. That is 100 bottles without you leaving your house. Treat your partners wellâgive them small gifts at Christmas, and always deliver on time.

lessons.title: Word-of-Mouth Marketing Strategies
lessons.body:
Word-of-mouth is the cheapest and most trusted marketing in Africa. One happy customer tells 5 friends. One angry customer tells 20. So your first job is to make every customer happy. Always give a small extraâa free 50ml sample, a handwritten thank-you note, or a small discount on their next buy. When someone buys, ask them directly: 'Please tell two friends who need this.' Give them two extra business cards to pass on. This simple ask doubles your reach.

Create a 'referral reward'. If a customer brings a new buyer, give them a free 250ml bottle or 10% off their next order. Track this in a notebook. When the new buyer comes, ask who sent them. Write it down. Then reward the referrer immediately. This encourages more referrals. Also, use your WhatsApp status. Post a photo of a happy customer (with their permission) and write 'Another satisfied customer in Ikeja!' People see this and trust you more.

Join community groupsâchurch, mosque, women's meetings, youth clubs. Offer to give a short talk on 'Natural Skin Care' and bring samples. At the end, sell your oils. These groups love to support their own. Also, barter with other small businesses: give a bottle of oil to a tailor, and ask them to wear your branded T-shirt or mention you to clients. Give a free jar of shea butter to a popular hairdresser. They will talk about you.

Never underestimate the power of a clean, consistent product. If your oil smells fresh and your shea butter is smooth, people will talk. But if quality drops, bad news travels faster. Always package in clean bottles with your phone number. Use a simple label. Ask for feedback: 'What can I improve?' When you fix a problem, tell the customer. They will become your biggest fan. Within a year, word-of-mouth can bring you 50% of your sales. It costs nothing but effort and honesty.

lessons.title: Handling Customer Complaints and Returns
lessons.body:
A complaint is a chance to keep a customer forever. Never argue. Listen first. If a customer says the oil smells bad or the shea butter is gritty, say, 'I am sorry. Let me fix this.' Ask for details: when did they buy, how was it stored, what is the batch number? If you don't have batch numbers, start using themâwrite a date on each bottle. If the product is truly bad, replace it immediately with a fresh one. Do not ask for a receipt if they are a known customer. The cost of one bottle is small compared to losing their trust.

For returns, have a clear policy: 'If you are not satisfied, return within 7 days for a replacement or refund.' Write this on your label or WhatsApp catalogue. When someone returns, smile and accept it. Ask them to try the new product. Give a small extra for the inconvenienceâa free lip balm or a 10% discount on their next order. This turns a bad experience into a good story. They will tell others how well you handled it.

If a customer complains publicly on WhatsApp or Facebook, reply politely in the same place. Say, 'I am sorry. Please send me a private message so I can make it right.' Then solve it quickly. Never delete their comment. Others are watching. If you solve it well, post a follow-up: 'Thank you for your patience. We have replaced your oil and added a free gift.' This shows you are honest.

Keep a complaint log. Write the date, customer name, problem, and solution. After one month, read it. If many people complain about the same thingâlike leaky bottlesâchange your supplier. If they complain about price, consider a smaller size. Use complaints to improve. Also, train anyone who helps you sell to follow the same rules. A customer who complains and is treated well becomes more loyal than one who never complained. In the end, your reputation for fairness will sell more oil than any advert.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Marketing and Selling Coconut Oil & Shea Oil Locally

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons of the Marketing and Selling Locally module into a working toolkit you can apply immediately. Whether you press coconut oil in Kilifi or hand-craft shea butter in Tamale, your route to revenue runs through the same channels: local markets and trade fairs, WhatsApp and social media, your own community, salons and cosmetic shops, word-of-mouth, and clean complaint handling. The goal is not just to sell once â it is to build repeatable, profitable demand for your oil.

1. Selling at Local Markets and Trade Fairs

Markets are your fastest route to first-time buyers, but competition is fierce. Differentiate with a clean, labelled bottle (even a recycled jar with a printed sticker), a visible sample, and a clear price. At trade fairs â such as the Nairobi International Trade Fair or regional agricultural shows â buyers expect to negotiate and to sample. Bring 100â200 small 50 ml trial bottles; they convert far better than large containers. Keep a simple sales book: date, quantity sold, price, and customer phone number. That book becomes your first customer database.

2. Using WhatsApp and Social Media to Sell

WhatsApp Business is the single most effective low-cost sales tool for African oil producers. Set up a Business profile with your location, catalogue, and a greeting message. Post 2â3 times weekly: product photos, a short video of the pressing process, customer testimonials, and price lists. Use WhatsApp Status for daily offers. On Facebook and Instagram, join local buy-and-sell groups and market pages. TikTok works well for short "how it's made" clips. Always respond within a few hours â speed builds trust.

3. Building a Customer Base in Your Community

Your neighbours, church or mosque members, market women, and local cooperatives are your first customers. Offer a small loyalty scheme: buy five bottles, get the sixth at half price. Record every customer's name and phone number. Host a monthly "oil day" at your workshop where people can see the process and buy directly. Community trust converts into referrals, which is cheaper than any advertising.

4. Partnering with Salons and Cosmetic Shops

Salons and beauty shops are high-leverage partners: they already have your target customers. Offer a wholesale price (typically 20â30% below retail), a small display stand, and free samples for stylists. Agree on a simple consignment or cash-on-delivery arrangement in writing. Provide branded labels and a short script the shop owner can use when recommending your oil. A single well-stocked salon can move 20â50 bottles a month.

5. Word-of-Mouth Marketing Strategies

Word-of-mouth is the cheapest and most powerful channel in African markets. Give every satisfied customer two extra sample sachets to share. Ask for a short testimonial you can post on WhatsApp Status. Offer a referral discount: when a customer brings a new buyer, both get 10% off the next purchase. Encourage customers to leave voice notes or short videos you can reshare. Consistency and honesty matter more than clever slogans.

6. Handling Customer Complaints and Returns

Complaints are opportunities. Adopt a three-step rule: listen, apologise, act. If the oil is rancid, leaking, or mislabelled, replace it immediately â no argument. Record the complaint in a log so you can trace the batch. Never blame the customer publicly. A customer whose complaint is handled well often becomes your most loyal promoter.

⚠ SAFETY WARNING: Never sell coconut or shea oil that has been stored in contaminated, rusted, or previously used chemical containers. Rancid oil (smells sour or bitter, feels sticky) can cause skin irritation and must be discarded, not sold. Always label bottles with production date, batch number, and ingredients. Keep oils away from direct sunlight and heat above 30Â°C. In markets, do not decant oil into unlabelled bottles for customers â this is both a health risk and a traceability failure. Follow your national standards authority guidance (e.g., KEBS in Kenya, SON in Nigeria, GSA in Ghana).

Quick Reference Checklist

  • ☐ Every bottle is labelled with product name, weight, production date, and batch number.
  • ☐ WhatsApp Business profile is complete with catalogue, location, and greeting message.
  • ☐ You post product content at least 3 times per week.
  • ☐ Customer names and phone numbers are recorded for every sale.
  • ☐ At least 2 salons or cosmetic shops have a written supply agreement.
  • ☐ A referral or loyalty incentive is active and communicated to customers.
  • ☐ A complaint log exists and every complaint is resolved within 48 hours.
  • ☐ Prices are reviewed monthly against local market rates and input costs.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • Global Shea Alliance â Resources & Business Handbooks

  • TechnoServe â Agribusiness Toolkits and Case Studies
  • ILO Value Chain Development â Market Linkage Guides
  • Agribusiness How It Works â Practical Guides for African Producers

Key takeaway: Marketing coconut and shea oil locally is not about big budgets â it is about consistency, trust, and systems. Label properly, post regularly, record every customer, partner with salons, reward referrals, and handle complaints fast. These habits turn a small pressing operation into a sustainable local brand.

quiz.q: What is the best first step before selling at a local market?
options: A) Buy a large stall immediately
B) Visit as a customer and study prices and competition
quiz.explanation: Visiting first helps you understand prices, customer flow, and what sells before you invest.

quiz.q: Why is a stall near the market entrance often worth the higher cost?
options: B) You sell three times more than at the back
quiz.explanation: High-traffic spots near the entrance attract more buyers, increasing sales volume.

quiz.q: At a trade fair, what should you do with people who stop by but don't buy?
options: B) Give them a free sample and collect their phone number
quiz.explanation: Collecting contacts lets you follow up later and turn them into customers.

quiz.q: What is a good way to handle change at a market stall?
options: B) Keep plenty of small notes and coins
C) Ask customers to bring exact change
quiz.explanation: Having small change speeds up sales and avoids losing customers who only have big notes.

quiz.q: How often should you send broadcast messages on WhatsApp to customers?
options: D) Only when you have new stock
quiz.explanation: Once a week is frequent enough to remind customers without annoying them.

quiz.q: What is a key feature of WhatsApp Business?
quiz.explanation: WhatsApp Business offers a catalogue, auto-replies, and labels to manage orders professionally.

quiz.q: Which social media platform is best for short, viral videos of your oil?
quiz.explanation: TikTok's short video format can reach many people quickly and go viral.

quiz.q: What should you do after a customer receives their order?
options: A) Ask for a photo review and post it
quiz.explanation: Photo reviews build trust and encourage others to buy.

quiz.q: How can you build a customer base in your community?
options: B) Give free samples to 50 people you know
C) Wait for customers to come to you
quiz.explanation: Personal sampling introduces your product and starts word-of-mouth.

quiz.q: What is a loyalty card?
options: A) A card that gives free products to everyone
B) A card that rewards repeat customers, e.g., buy 5 get 1 free
C) A card for wholesale buyers only
quiz.explanation: Loyalty cards encourage repeat purchases by offering a reward after a set number of buys.

quiz.q: Why should you record every sale?
options: B) To identify your best customers and products
quiz.explanation: Sales records help you understand what sells and who buys most, so you can focus your efforts.

quiz.q: What is a good way to turn customers into fans?
options: A) Host a sampling day with special prices
quiz.explanation: Sampling days create a personal connection and encourage bulk buying.

quiz.q: When partnering with a salon, what wholesale discount should you offer?
quiz.explanation: A 30% discount gives the salon a good profit margin while keeping your price fair.

quiz.q: What is consignment?
options: A) Selling all stock at once
B) Giving stock to a shop to sell, and you get paid after they sell
quiz.explanation: Consignment means the shop pays you only after selling the product, reducing their risk.

quiz.q: Why should you provide an invoice book to salon partners?
options: B) To avoid disputes over stock and payments
quiz.explanation: A signed invoice records what was given and sold, preventing misunderstandings.

quiz.q: What is a 'salon exclusive' scent?
options: A) A scent only you sell to that salon
D) A scent for men only
quiz.explanation: Exclusive scents make the salon feel special and give them a unique selling point.

quiz.q: How can you motivate salon workers to recommend your product?
options: A) Give them free products for personal use
D) Ask them to work for free
quiz.explanation: Happy workers who use and like your product will naturally recommend it to clients.

quiz.q: What is the cheapest and most trusted marketing method in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Personal recommendations from satisfied customers are highly trusted and cost nothing.

quiz.q: What should you do when a customer buys from you?
options: A) Ask them to tell two friends and give them extra cards
C) Raise the price next time
quiz.explanation: Directly asking for referrals doubles your reach with little effort.

quiz.q: What is a referral reward?
options: A) A discount for new customers only
B) A gift or discount for a customer who brings a new buyer
C) A free product for everyone
D) A penalty for not referring
quiz.explanation: Rewarding referrers encourages them to bring more new customers.

quiz.q: Why should you join community groups like church or women's meetings?
options: A) To give a talk and sell your oils
quiz.explanation: These groups are supportive and provide a captive audience for your products.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do when a customer complains?
quiz.explanation: Listening and apologising shows respect and opens the door to solving the problem.

quiz.q: What should you do if a product is truly bad?
options: A) Replace it immediately with a fresh one
D) Tell them to buy again
quiz.explanation: Replacing bad products quickly keeps the customer's trust and loyalty.

quiz.q: What is a good return policy to have?
options: B) Return within 7 days for replacement or refund
C) Return within 30 days only if unopened
D) Returns only for wholesale buyers
quiz.explanation: A clear, generous return policy reduces customer risk and builds confidence.

quiz.q: How should you handle a public complaint on Facebook?
options: B) Reply politely and ask them to send a private message
quiz.explanation: A polite public reply shows others you care, and moving to private solves the issue without drama.

quiz.q: Why keep a complaint log?
options: A) To identify common problems and improve
quiz.explanation: Reviewing complaints helps you fix recurring issues and improve your product.

quiz.q: What should you do if many customers complain about leaky bottles?
quiz.explanation: Fixing the root cause by finding better bottles prevents future complaints.

quiz.q: What is the best way to handle a return?
options: A) Accept it with a smile and give a small extra
D) Tell them to come back later
quiz.explanation: A positive return experience turns a dissatisfied customer into a loyal one.

quiz.q: How can you turn a complaint into a good story?
options: A) Solve it quickly and post a follow-up thanking the customer
quiz.explanation: Publicly showing you resolved a complaint builds trust with other potential customers.

quiz.q: What should you do to prevent disputes with salon partners?
options: A) Use a signed invoice book
quiz.explanation: A signed invoice book provides a clear record of transactions and prevents misunderstandings.
